metadata.note: The Illinois Terminal Railroad — the Illinois Traction System until 1937 — was the largest interurban network in the Midwest outside Ohio and Indiana, some 550 miles at its height and still 462 route miles in 1950, radiating from Springfield to St. Louis, Peoria, Bloomington, Decatur, Champaign and Danville. William B. McKinley built it from 1901 onward, beginning with a short line from Danville to Westville in October 1901, and it was unusual among interurbans in almost everything: it was originally electrified at 3,300 volts single-phase AC before being converted to 650-volt DC around 1910, it built its own bridge over the Mississippi — the McKinley Bridge, opened to the cars on 1 October 1910 — to reach downtown St. Louis rather than pay a rival, it carried heavy carload freight as well as passengers, and it is remembered for running sleeping cars, a thing almost no other interurban attempted. The passenger network came apart in stages: the small Danville branches went in the 1920s and 1930s, the Bloomington routes and the Danville–Champaign line in 1953, Decatur–Springfield and Champaign–Decatur in 1955, and interurban passenger service ended altogether on 3 March 1956. Only the St. Louis–Granite City suburban trains ran on, to 21 June 1958. Freight lasted far longer, into the Norfolk Southern era, but none of those years are drawn here.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois_Terminal_Railroad — the twelve-route table with opening and closing years used for almost every segment's end date, the 3 March 1956 end of interurban passenger service, the 1958 end of St. Louis–Granite City commuter service, the 3,300 V AC to 650 V DC re-electrification around 1910, the 550-mile system size, and the McKinley Bridge.

https://www.american-rails.com/it.html — precise opening dates (Danville–Westville 20 October 1901, Catlin 29 May 1902, Georgetown 27 August 1902, Champaign 6 September 1903, Springfield–Decatur 25 September 1904, Ridge Farm 1 October 1905, St. Louis & Springfield and St. Louis & North Eastern 16 February 1906, Decatur–Bloomington 1 August 1906, Bloomington–Peoria via Mackinaw 21 April 1907, Lincoln–Mackinaw 1 January 1908, McKinley Bridge 1 October 1910), the 1930 Alton acquisition, the 462 route miles of 1950 and the 21 June 1958 end of suburban service.

https://pantagraph.com/special-section/news/history-and-events/04-12-09-bloomington-once-a-stop-on-electric-railway-system/article_d6bb0165-4806-578a-9f55-f788b64840dc.html — the six cities served and the 1948 figure of 48 stops on the 37-mile Peoria–Bloomington run.

OpenStreetMap ways tagged old_railway_operator=IT / 'Illinois Terminal' / 'Illinois Traction' — the source of all real geometry in this file: the Madison County Transit trails, the McKinley Bridge, the Alton District, and the razed main line from Worden through Staunton, Carlinville and Girard to Springfield and east toward Illiopolis.
not_yet_sourced: GEOMETRY: seven features (Decatur–Champaign, Champaign–Danville, Decatur–Bloomington, Bloomington–Peoria, Springfield–Peoria, Staunton–Hillsboro, Danville–Ridge Farm, Danville–Catlin) are straight lines between documented towns, not traced alignments. Nothing in OpenStreetMap east or north of Springfield carries an Illinois Terminal operator tag, and corridor routing over the surviving abandoned grades produced the Baltimore and Ohio, Illinois Central and Wabash alignments instead. These are the highest-value targets for re-tracing.

DATE CONFLICTS between the Wikipedia route table and american-rails.com, in every case resolved here by drawing the LATER opening year: Springfield–Granite City 1904 vs February 1906; Danville–Champaign 1902 vs September 1903; Decatur–Bloomington 1905 vs August 1906; Danville–Ridge Farm 1901 vs October 1905 (1901 is the Westville opening).

The Alton branch: american-rails.com dates the acquisition to 1930, and the Wikipedia route table omits Alton entirely. Earlier electric passenger service on the Alton–Edwardsville corridor under predecessor companies is neither confirmed nor drawn.
The interurban sleeping cars, for which this railroad is best known, are described in the layer note but no source consulted here gives the years, the route or the last night they ran.

The affiliated city streetcar systems in Springfield, Decatur, Danville, Champaign-Urbana, Peoria and Alton are NOT drawn. No route geometry or electrification and closure dates were found for any of them. They would be mode 'streetcar' if added, and several of them began under animal power, so Rule 5 would require drawing them from electrification rather than from the founding of the company.
All headway_min values are estimates; no Illinois Terminal public timetable was consulted for any segment.
Route mileages: no per-route documented mileage was found except the 37-mile Peoria–Bloomington figure, so traced-vs-documented comparison is only possible for that one line.
metadata.horsecar_audit: No animal-powered operation is drawn. Every feature here is an interurban route built new as an electric railway from 1901 onward. The company's affiliated city streetcar systems, several of which did begin with mules, are deliberately not drawn at all (see not_yet_sourced).
metadata.freight_only_audit: The Illinois Terminal was a serious freight carrier and hauled carload freight for decades after the interurbans stopped — the last passenger service of any kind was the St. Louis–Granite City suburban run, which ended 21 June 1958. No feature in this file is drawn past its own route's last passenger year, and none past 1958.
metadata.interurban_audit: Every feature is mode 'interurban': all are inter-city electric railway routes. The street trackage in St. Louis, Venice, Madison and Springfield is drawn as part of the interurban routes it served, not as local city service. The company's genuinely local city streetcar systems are not drawn.

properties.line: Illinois Terminal: St. Louis – Granite City
properties.speed_source: Estimate. Illinois Traction limiteds were timed at roughly 40 mph over the road; the figures here are averages including stops, not documented schedule speeds.
properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=IT — the McKinley Bridge and its bikeway, the Trestle, Broadway, McCambridge and Madison Avenue street trackage through Venice and Madison — with 1.2 mi of straight-line connector where the approach tracks in St. Louis have gone. Traced 5.6 mi.

segments.note: The McKinley Bridge, built by the Illinois Traction System's own promoter William B. McKinley and opened to the railway on 1 October 1910, gave the interurban its own crossing of the Mississippi and a downtown St. Louis terminal. This was the last passenger service the company ran: the St. Louis–Granite City suburban trains outlived the through interurbans by two years and stopped on 21 June 1958. Headway is an estimate for the suburban service; through interurban trains were far less frequent.
sources: Segment-level: the 1 October 1910 McKinley Bridge opening and the 21 June 1958 end of St. Louis–Granite City suburban service are from american-rails.com; the Wikipedia route table gives the same 1910–1958 span for Granite City–St. Louis.

properties.geometry_quality: The best geometry in this file. Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=IT / 'Illinois Terminal' / 'Illinois Traction' — the Madison County Transit trails (Nature, Goshen, Quercus Grove, Schoolhouse) on the right of way south of Edwardsville and a long chain of razed IT ways north through Worden, Staunton, Carlinville and Girard to the eastern edge of Springfield — with about 4.9 mi of straight-line connector spread over ten gaps. APPROXIMATED LEG: the last 1.7 mi into the Springfield terminal at 5th and Jefferson is a single straight segment, that stretch having been street trackage which is not mapped. Traced 97.3 mi; no documented Granite City–Springfield mileage was located for comparison.

segments.note: The Wikipedia route table dates Springfield–Granite City 1904–1956; american-rails.com dates the St. Louis & Springfield line to Staunton and the St. Louis & North Eastern to Granite City both to 16 February 1906. The later date is used here so the drawn years do not assert service before it is agreed to have run — the conflict is recorded in metadata.not_yet_sourced. This was the system's trunk, carrying the through St. Louis–Springfield–Peoria trains. Interurban passenger service over it ended on 3 March 1956. Headway is an estimate.
sources: Segment-level: the 3 March 1956 end of interurban passenger service is from the Wikipedia article; the 1906 opening dates are from american-rails.com and conflict with Wikipedia's 1904.

properties.geometry_quality: PART TRACED, PART STRAIGHT LINE. The western 17.4 mi out of Springfield is traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator='Illinois Terminal' with no connectors at all — genuinely the railroad's own alignment. The 1.7 mi from the Springfield terminal to the start of that trace, and the eastern 21 mi from Illiopolis into Decatur, are straight segments: the grade east of Illiopolis is not identifiable in OpenStreetMap. Drawn length 38.8 mi.

segments.note: Opened 25 September 1904, the first of the Illinois Traction's long interurban routes and the spine of the eastern system. Passenger service ended in 1955. Headway is an estimate.

properties.geometry_quality: Traced from OSM ways tagged old_railway_operator=IT — the Alton District (A&E Line) and the Sam Vadalabene Trail — with 0.3 mi of straight-line connector. Traced 15.4 mi. Note that some of the IT-tagged track here is freight-era Alton District trackage; whether the passenger interurban used exactly this alignment for its whole length was not verified.

segments.note: american-rails.com states the Alton branch was acquired in 1930 to give the system access to Alton. Electric railways had served the Alton–Edwardsville corridor earlier under other companies, but neither their years nor whether the Illinois Terminal ran passengers over this line before 1930 was established, so the drawn years start at the acquisition. Ends with the 3 March 1956 close of interurban passenger service. Headway is an estimate.
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: american-rails.com gives the 1930 acquisition, but no source was checked for Illinois Terminal passenger service on this branch, its frequency, or its last year. The Wikipedia route table has no Alton entry at all.

properties.geometry_quality: STRAIGHT-LINE APPROXIMATION. No Illinois Terminal alignment is identifiable in OpenStreetMap along this corridor — nothing carries old_railway_operator=IT east or north of Springfield, and routing over the surviving abandoned grades put the line on the B&O, the Illinois Central or the Wabash instead, which would have been worse than a straight line. This feature is therefore drawn as straight segments between the towns the route is documented to have served; intermediate stations and every curve are missing. Length below is the straight-line length, not the railroad's mileage. Drawn 42.2 mi straight.

segments.note: Springfield north to Lincoln opened in 1906; the Lincoln–Mackinaw connector opened on New Year's Day 1908, completing the through Springfield–Peoria route and joining the Bloomington line at Mackinaw. The whole feature is drawn from 1908, when the route it represents could first be ridden end to end. This was one of the last two interurban routes running, to 3 March 1956. Headway is an estimate.
